docs.title: firescript Philosophy
docs.text: firescript is intended to be a simple but powerful and fast language with safety by design. This is accomplished through a strict type system, explicit design, and simple to learn but powerful compile-time memory management.

docs.title: Key Principles
docs.text:
• Simplicity: The language syntax and semantics are designed to be easy to learn and understand, minimizing complexity while maximizing expressiveness.
  • Safety: Strong static typing, null safety, and compile-time checks help prevent common programming errors.
  • Null safety is enforced by default; nullable types must be explicitly declared.
  • Memory safety is ensured through compile-time ownership and borrowing rules, preventing issues like dangling pointers
  • There is no undefined behavior; all operations are well-defined.
  • Performance: Although the syntax is high-level, firescript is designed to compile to efficient low-level code, with no runtime overhead.
  • Explicitness: The language favors explicit declarations and operations over implicit behavior, making code easier to read and reason about.
  • Determinism: The compiler is fully deterministic — compiling the same source (and inputs) twice, on the same machine, must always produce byte-identical output. There is no reliance on hash-randomized iteration order, uninitialized memory, wall-clock time, or other non-reproducible state anywhere in the pipeline.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.13+ (firescript generally targets the latest version of Python)

No C compiler, assembler, or linker is required — the firescript compiler assembles x86-64 machine code and writes the executable itself using only the Python standard library.

Supported Platforms: - Windows (x86_64)

Note: The compiler is developed on Windows. As it is currently under active development, there may be platform-specific issues. If you encounter any problems on your platform, please report them in the issue tracker. Contributions to improve cross-platform compatibility are also welcome.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Clone the repository

git clone https://github.com/alec-jensen/firescript.git
cd firescript

docs.title: Compiling and Running a Program
docs.text:
# Compile a firescript program (output goes to build\program.exe)
python firescript/main.py program.fire

# Execute the compiled program
.\build\program.exe

Useful flags:

  • -o <path> — choose the output file
  • -d — debug output
  • --check — run checks only, without generating code
  • --emit {ast,asm,obj,bin} — choose the kind of output to generate

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: This glossary contains definitions of terms commonly used in the firescript documentation. For authoritative rules on ownership and lifetimes see Memory Management.

docs.title: Memory Management Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Copyable Fixed-size value with no destructor; copied bitwise. Owned Resource/heap-managing value with unique ownership semantics. Move Transfer of ownership; original binding becomes invalid. Borrow (&T) Read-only, non-owning view whose lifetime is limited to an expression or call boundary. Clone Explicit duplication of an owned value’s contents (deep or COW per type). Drop Deterministic destruction at an inserted point (last use or scope exit). Module A piece of firescript code that is imported or included in another firescript file. Package A module or collection of modules that is installed via the package manager. Library A module or collection of modules that is provided with the firescript installation.

docs.title: Expanded Definitions
docs.text:
• Copyable: Includes intN, floatN, bool, and char. These are fixed-size scalars stored on the stack. Copies are bitwise; no destructor runs.
  • Owned: Includes user-defined objects, closures, arrays, and strings. These values are stored on the heap with pointers on the stack. Ownership is unique unless an explicit sharing container (future Rc, Arc) is used.
  • Move: Occurs on assignment, passing to a parameter of owned type, or returning a value. After a move, the source binding cannot be used (use-after-move error).
  • Borrow: Lightweight, read-only access. Cannot be stored in owned fields or escape its originating scope/call. Does not incur runtime overhead.
  • Clone: Creates an independent owned value (planned; explicit .clone() is not yet implemented). Semantics (deep vs copy-on-write) determined by the type implementation but always preserves logical independence.
  • Drop: Compiler-inserted destructor invocation (drop(this)) ensuring timely resource release (files, sockets, buffers) without tracing GC.
  • Module: A single .fire file or a collection of files that can be imported. Modules encapsulate code and can expose public APIs.
  • Package: A distributable unit of code, often hosted in a package registry. Packages can contain multiple modules and dependencies.
  • Library: A set of pre-written modules provided with the firescript installation, offering standard functionality (e.g., std.io, std.math).

docs.title: Internal Documentation
docs.text: This is documentation for internal language features intended for use in the compiler and standard library. These are not intended for use in user code, as these features require careful handling to be used safely and correctly.

docs.title: Compiler internals
docs.text:
FIR + FLIR Pipeline - Index for the FIR (firescript Intermediate Representation) and FLIR (firescript Lowered Intermediate Representation) design docs: architecture overview, per-IR specs, and a developer quick reference. [IMPLEMENTED]

Native Toolchain - How the self-hosted x86-64 assembler and PE32+ writer work. [IMPLEMENTED]

float128 - The self-hosted IEEE 754 binary128 float128 type and its soft-float runtime. [IMPLEMENTED]

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Language model redesign - Design for the 1.0 memory model (value semantics, move, &T/&mut T), const, visibility, the object model (interfaces, abstract classes, Object), primitive bindings, and function interfaces. [PLANNED]

Specification and versioning - Terminology (firescript Language Specification fls, firescript Compiler fsc), independent semantic versioning, the fls/fsc/kiln compatibility contract, and how to prepare for spec-version gating. [PLANNED]

Fuzzing and edge-case testing plan - Planned fuzz targets, oracles, and edge-case matrices. [PLANNED]

Version planning - Release roadmap toward 1.0.0.

docs.title: Directives
docs.text:
Directives - Internal directives for controlling compiler behavior, used in the standard library and for testing. Not intended for user code.

Syscall Directive - Internal directive for defining syscalls, used in the standard library to define OS-level syscalls. Not intended for user code.

docs.title: Test audit
docs.text: Test suite audit (snapshot at cfdae0d) - Consolidated findings of a read-only audit of the test suite: redundant, weak and incorrect tests, deduplicated compiler bugs, docs-vs-compiler conflicts, and a cleanup plan. Raw per-shard reports live alongside it.

docs.title: compiler directives
docs.text:
compiler directives are special instructions to the compiler that affect compilation behavior. They are not part of the runtime language and do not produce any code themselves.

Directives are not intended to be used in source files except in specific scenarios (e.g., enabling syscalls in the standard library). They are primarily for internal use by the compiler and standard library.

docs.title: Directive Syntax
docs.text:
directive <name> [<arg1> [, <arg2> ...]];
  • directive keyword starts the directive.
  • <name> is the name of the directive (e.g., enable_syscalls).
  • Optional arguments can be provided, separated by commas.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Enable syscalls in a file:
directive enable_syscalls;
  • Enable compiler-inserted drops (preprocessor inserts drop() calls):

Should ONLY be used internally by the preprocessor.

directive enable_drops;
  • Enable process argument intrinsics (process_argc / process_argv_at):
directive enable_process_args;

docs.title: Available Directives
docs.text:
• enable_syscalls: Allows the use of syscalls in the file. This is required for files in the standard library that need syscall access (e.g. std.io).
  • enable_drops: Enables the preprocessor to insert deterministic drop() calls for Owned values (e.g., arrays) at scope boundaries and early exits.
  • enable_lowlevel_stdout: Allows the use of low-level stdout function.
  • enable_lowlevel_stdin: Allows the use of low-level stdin function.
  • enable_process_args: Allows use of process argument intrinsics (process_argc() and process_argv_at(index)) and low-level string helper intrinsics (str_length, str_char_at, str_index_of, str_slice) in the file. This is intended for standard library internals (for example, std.cli.args).
  • enable_lowlevel_runtime: Allows use of the runtime-implementation primitives. Exclusively for firescript/std/internal/*.fire (the firescript-implemented runtime, split by concern across several files -- alloc.fire, strings.fire, number_conversions.fire, float_conversions.fire, io.fire, syscalls.fire, etc. -- all merged into every program built with the FIR backends; any of these files may call any other's functions with no import between them). Primitives:
  • Raw memory: mem_load_u8(addr) -> uint8, mem_store_u8(addr, v), mem_load_u64(addr) -> uint64, mem_store_u64(addr, v), mem_copy(dst, src, n) — addresses are uint64.
  • Bitcasts: str_to_addr(string) -> uint64, addr_to_str(uint64) -> string.
  • Runtime state: runtime_state_get() -> uint64 / runtime_state_set(uint64) — a single mutable pointer-sized cell holding the runtime's root state block.
  • Win32 externs (lower to kernel32.dll imports): win_get_process_heap, win_heap_alloc, win_heap_free, win_get_std_handle, win_write_file, win_read_file, win_create_file_a, win_close_handle, win_delete_file_a, win_move_file_ex_a, win_copy_file_a, win_get_last_error, win_get_command_line_a, win_get_file_size, win_exit_process. Handles and pointers are uint64.

Functions in the runtime module named fs_rt_* implement the FLIR runtime ABI; the FIR lowering routes runtime calls to them when defined, falling back to backend-provided shims otherwise (which allows incremental porting). - enable_builtin_methods: Allows the @builtin_method("family", "name", **flags) decorator on a function declaration. Exclusively for firescript/std/internal/*.fire. The decorated function becomes the backing implementation of a dot-method (.name()) on every value of the given receiver family ("string", "array") across every compiled program, with no user import -- see firescript/builtin_methods.py for the registry that scans for these at compile time, and its docstring / firescript/std/internal/strings.fire and builtin_arrays.fire for authoring examples.

docs.title: language model redesign (toward 1.0)
docs.text: Status: [PLANNED] — design document. Nothing described here is implemented unless it says so explicitly. All syntax is provisional. The roadmap that schedules this work is version_planning.md. Until each part ships, the user-facing docs under /docs/reference remain the source of truth for what the compiler does today.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
firescript's memory model grew from a Python-shaped intuition: two categories of type (Copyable and Owned) where the category decides what a = b means. Experience with C++ and Rust suggests a better foundation: every type is a value, copying is the default, moving and borrowing are explicit. The same pass covers const-correctness, member visibility, and an OOP model that reads like Java but compiles to flat, statically dispatched code.

Where this document says "today", it describes the compiler as audited in November 2026.

docs.title: 1.1 Every type is a value
docs.text:
There is no Owned/Copyable split visible to users. Every type is a value; classes are stored inline (like C++ objects), not behind an implicit heap pointer.

  • a = b and passing an argument by value copy the value, memberwise.
  • A copy of a trivially copyable type (primitives, classes whose fields are all trivially copyable) is a bitwise copy and has no cleanup.
  • A class's copy copies each field using that field's own copy. Types that manage a buffer (string, Vec<T>, fixed arrays of such) define their copy as a deep copy.
  • A class may define its own deep-copy hook (first-party, like a C++ copy constructor). Name and syntax are open (copy(&this) -> T is the working assumption).
  • A class with a field that cannot be copied is move-only unless it defines a copy. Example: a File handle. This is derived by the compiler; users never write a category.
class Point { x: int32; y: int32; }          // trivially copyable (derived)
class Doc    { title: string; tags: Vec<string>; } // copyable, copy is deep (derived from fields)
class Handle { file: File; }                 // move-only (File has no copy)

p: Point = Point(1, 2);
q: Point = p;            // copy
d: Doc = Doc(...);
e: Doc = d;              // copy (deep, via string/Vec copy)
h: Handle = open(...);
k: Handle = h;           // error: Handle cannot be copied; use move
k: Handle = move h;      // ok

docs.title: 1.2 Move is explicit
docs.text: move x transfers the value out of x; x is unusable afterward (use-after-move is still a compile error, via the existing move-state analysis). The exact spelling (move x vs move(x)) is open. Returning a local by value is an implicit move.

docs.title: 1.3 Drops
docs.text: Deterministic, compiler-inserted destruction is unchanged in spirit. A type needs a destructor if it, or any field, manages a resource; the compiler derives this. The @owns_elements class decorator used by Vec today becomes derivable from field types.

docs.title: 1.4 Internal predicates
docs.text: The compiler keeps three internal predicates (never user keywords): trivially copyable, needs destructor, copyable. Diagnostics speak in terms of "cannot be copied; use move".

docs.title: 1.5 Consequences
docs.text:
• copyable class is removed.
  • CopyableOption / CopyableResult / CopyableTuple collapse into Option / Result / Tuple.
  • The "cannot borrow a Copyable type" rule is removed.
  • The planned Owned / Copyable generic constraints are dropped. Generics stay monomorphized; generic code that copies a T is checked at instantiation.
  • Passing a large value by value copies it. Convention: take &T for read-only parameters. A lint for large implicit copies is a candidate.
  • Class layout in FLIR lowering changes from heap-pointer to inline.

docs.title: 2.1 Syntax and kinds
docs.text:
• &T — shared, read-only reference (transitively const; see §4).
  • &mut T — mutable reference, exclusive.
  • Receivers keep &this and &mut this. Today a parameter is written &name: T; moving the & into the type is open, and the docs/parser mismatch should be resolved with this change.

docs.title: 2.2 Exclusivity
docs.text: While a &mut to a value is live, no other reference to it (shared or mutable) is live. Checked over lexical scope (no full non-lexical-lifetime analysis initially). Today there is no exclusivity check at all.

docs.title: 2.3 Where references may appear
docs.text:
• Allowed as parameters and locals.
  • A reference may be returned only if it is derived from a reference parameter or this (elision: with one reference input the output borrows from it; &this methods may return borrows of their fields). No lifetime annotations.
  • References cannot be stored in fields for now. Never returning or storing a reference to a local is what makes dangling references impossible.

Returning a value by value is always fine and is a move: the caller receives ownership.

docs.title: 2.4 Deferred pointer-like types
docs.text: Box<T> (unique heap ownership, needed for recursive types and owned polymorphism) and Shared<T> (reference counted, the explicit opt-in to dynamic lifetime) are planned stdlib types but are not part of the first cut. There are no raw pointers. Until Box exists, recursive types (lists, trees) and owned polymorphic values are not expressible.

docs.title: 3. Const [PLANNED]
docs.text:
Today const on a local or class field is parsed but not enforced, and const class fields do not parse. (Top-level literal constants work.) The redesign:

  • Binding const: const x: T = e; forbids reassigning x.
  • Object const: access through &T is read-only and transitive: no field assignment, no calling a method that takes &mut this, through any depth of owned fields. Through Box it stays deep; through Shared mutation requires an explicit opt-in.
  • Const methods: &this methods are the const methods. A &T can call them; it cannot call &mut this methods.
  • Const fields are assignable only in the constructor.
  • References are not reseatable, so no "const pointer vs pointer to const" distinction exists.
  • A mutable field escape hatch (C++ style, for caches) is out of scope for now.

Const and exclusivity are one mechanism (shared vs mutable access) and are implemented together.

docs.title: 4. Visibility [PLANNED]
docs.text: Class members get private, protected, and public, modeled on C++ (default and exact semantics to be decided; module-level export is unchanged). Today there is no member visibility. This is a semantic-analyzer check with no backend impact.

docs.title: 5. Classes, abstract classes, interfaces, Object [PLANNED]
docs.text:
Java-style, not C++-style.

  • class — concrete; single inheritance.
  • abstract class — may have fields, concrete methods, and abstract methods; not instantiable.
  • interface — methods only (abstract, plus defaults), no fields; a class implements many.
  • Object — every class derives from Object; it supplies the common methods (working set: toString, equals, hashCode).

docs.title: 5.1 Making it cheap
docs.text:
• Classes are inline flat structs; methods are plain functions taking a receiver; calls are static by default.
  • A vtable pointer exists only in classes whose hierarchy has a method that is overridden and reached through dynamic dispatch. Because firescript is a whole-program compiler, it can see every subclass and devirtualize any method nothing overrides. Object as a root is therefore mostly a type-system relationship, not a per-object tax.
  • Interfaces default to static dispatch: fn f<T: Comparable>(x: T) is monomorphized. Dynamic dispatch goes through &Interface (a fat reference: data pointer plus vtable pointer).
  • Polymorphism is through references (and later Box), never by value, so there is no slicing. Consequence: a bare Shape s = Circle(...) for an abstract Shape is an error; use &Shape.
  • Single inheritance with the base laid out as a prefix.

docs.title: 5.2 Today
docs.text: Inheritance (class D from B) is a parse-time copy-down of base fields and methods with static overriding; there are no vtables, no subtyping, no abstract classes, no interfaces. Interface names in generic constraints are parsed as type names only. docs/reference/classes.md documents overriding as working; without dispatch it works only statically.

docs.title: 5.3 Primitives and Object
docs.text: A bare int32 has no header, so it cannot be viewed as &Object without boxing (as in Java). Until Box exists, primitives get Object's methods statically through bindings (§6) but are not dynamically Objects.

docs.title: 6. Primitive bindings [PLANNED]
docs.text:
Binding a library class to a primitive type lets a.abs() work on an int32.

@bind(int32)
class Integer32 : Integer {
    fn abs(this: int32) -> int32 { ... }
}
  • The binding directive is enabled only for the standard library. (Today, directives are not actually restricted to std: any user file can write directive enable_lowlevel_runtime;. Gating needs to be enforced as part of this work. Only @builtin_method is path-restricted today.)
  • a.abs() lowers to a static call Integer32.abs(a): zero runtime cost.
  • The compiler keeps a binding table (type to class). A method call on a primitive resolves through it and implicitly loads the defining module; no import is required. Module load order must be deterministic (source order, never table iteration order).
  • Integer is an interface implemented by each binding (Integer8 … Integer64, unsigned variants), not a base class, so no boxing is needed. Code that accepts any precision is generic: fn f<T: Integer>(x: T).
  • Today @builtin_method covers only the string and array families; there is no int or float family. The bindings replace and generalize it.

docs.title: 7. Function interfaces and lambdas [PLANNED]
docs.text:
interface fn Callback(a: int32, b: float64) -> void;
  • An interface fn is an interface with exactly one abstract method. A function or lambda with a matching signature converts to it. Matching is structural (no implements on a lambda), unlike classes, which are nominal.
  • An inline anonymous form (fn(int32, float64) -> void) is sugar; the named form is an alias.
  • Generic function interfaces use existing monomorphization (interface fn Mapper<T, R>(x: T) -> R;).
  • Dispatch follows §5.1: a by-value Callback parameter is generic over the concrete closure type (monomorphized, inlinable); &Callback is a fat reference.
  • Captures: non-capturing lambdas and plain functions are a bare function pointer. Capturing lambdas are an anonymous struct holding the captures (borrowed, or copied/moved in). Mutability falls out of the receiver rules: calling through &Callback needs a closure that does not mutate its captures; a mutating closure needs &mut Callback; a closure that consumes a moved-in value is taken by value and callable once.
  • Escaping closures (returned or stored) need heap storage and therefore Box; the first version allows only non-escaping closures that borrow from the enclosing scope. This extends the existing sketch in docs/reference/memory_management.md §5.
  • Today there are no lambdas, function values, or function types (type_system.md marks function types [PLANNED]).
  • Python-style function and class wrappers (decorators) are a later goal. They are intended to expand at compile time so they stay zero-cost and do not require escaping closures.

docs.title: 8.1 Replacing as
docs.text:
Once primitive bindings (§6) exist, the as cast keyword is removed. Today as handles numeric conversions, built-ins to string, and string to numeric ("42" as int32).

  • To string: x.toString() (from Object, or the primitive's binding).
  • Numeric conversions are methods on the bound class with the target in the name, e.g. a.toInt64(), f.toInt32(). Each states its semantics (a truncating conversion and a rounding one are different methods), and generic code can use an interface bound such as T: Number and call x.toFloat64().
  • String to number is a parse method that returns a Result, so failure is expressible.
  • Open: whether lossless widening (e.g. int32 to int64) is implicit. Lossy or fallible conversions are always explicit.
  • as stays until bindings ship and is then deprecated.

docs.title: 8.2 Membership
docs.text: There is no in operator beyond for x in y. Membership is a library call (contains), e.g. a method on an Iterable/Container interface. This keeps the cost visible and avoids a grammar ambiguity with for-in.

docs.title: 8.3 Runtime type tests
docs.text:
Library methods on Object, not keywords:

  • x.isInstance<T>() — true if x is a T or any subclass; for an interface T, true if the class implements it.
  • x.isExactly<T>() — true only if the concrete type is exactly T; rejected at compile time for an interface or abstract class T. Needed for symmetric equals() implementations.
  • x.downcast<T>() — returns Option<&T> using the isInstance rule (there is no nullable reference; see §12). This requires an Option that can hold a reference; whether it can is an open question for the &T work.

Cost: exact check compares a type ID; the class is-a check is an O(1) range test over a depth-first numbering of the single-inheritance hierarchy (the whole program is known); interface is-a checks consult a per-class interface table. A class used with these methods counts as dynamically used and gets a vtable pointer (§5.1).

An is keyword with a flow-narrowing binding (if (s is Circle c) { ... }) is deferred. It is the one thing a function cannot do; it is added later only if downcast plus a null check proves too clumsy in real code. The instanceof-style check is deliberately not a getClass/Class object: that would add a reflection concept.

docs.title: 9. Errors and exceptions [PLANNED]
docs.text: Today there is no catchable error mechanism. std.fs returns FileResult objects, Result<T,E> and Option<T> exist as library types, and runtime traps (integer overflow, division by zero, out-of-range indexing, invalid float-to-int conversions) print a message and terminate the program (docs/reference/error_handling.md). The design below is for 0.9.0, after the object model (§5) it depends on.

docs.title: 9.1 The rule: operations throw, function calls return a Result
docs.text:
There is exactly one way to signal each kind of failure:

  • Operations throw. A language operation that can fail raises an exception: integer overflow (+ - * / % **, unary minus, ++/--), division and modulo by zero, array indexing out of bounds, a float-to-int cast of NaN/infinity/out-of-range, and so on. These are the runtime traps of docs/reference/error_handling.md, made catchable.
  • Function calls return a Result. A function that can fail returns Result<T, E> (or Option<T> when there is no error to report). A function that cannot fail returns a plain value. Fallibility is visible in the signature and never raised behind the caller's back.
  • Exceptions are rooted at Exception extends Object, with a message and an optional cause, in a Python-style hierarchy: Exception -> ArithmeticException -> OverflowException, DivisionByZeroException; IndexOutOfBoundsException; InvalidConversionException; and so on. try { } catch (T e) { } finally { } matches by runtime type (the isInstance rule of §8.3), so catch (ArithmeticException e) catches the whole subtree. Syntax is provisional.
  • An exception raised inside a callee propagates through its callers until caught (an overflow deep in a call chain is still an exception), so callers do not need to be Result-aware of operations inside callees.
  • Catching a trap is the programmer acknowledging they will handle it; not catching it terminates the program with a stack trace (§9.3). A blanket catch (Exception e) is legal but discouraged, and a lint warns on it.
  • The same hierarchy classifies errors carried in a Result: Result<File, FileOpenException> (FileOpenException -> IOException -> Exception) is an ordinary error value, not something that is thrown. std.fs opening a file returns such a Result.
  • The runtime-trap work that precedes exceptions routes every trap through one runtime entry point so that it can later throw instead of exiting.

docs.title: 9.2 Consequences and open questions
docs.text:
• Ergonomics of Result everywhere. If every fallible call returns a Result, propagating an error through several calls needs a short form. A propagation operator (a postfix ? or a try-expression that returns early with the error) is strongly recommended; without it, every call site needs an explicit match. Open.
  • unwrap() and friends. Result.unwrap() cannot return a value when the result is an error. Proposal: it raises an exception (UnwrapException carrying the error), as the one explicit, named bridge from a Result to an exception. Open.
  • Collections. list.get(i) is a function, so under the rule it returns an Option/Result. Indexing with list[i] would be an operation and would throw. That points at an indexing interface (Indexable) so collections support []; open for 0.9.0.
  • No user-written throw statement in the initial design. Exceptions come from operations. Whether a catch block can rethrow (throw e;) is open.
  • Naming. Explicit arithmetic functions follow the same rule: wrapping_*/saturating_* cannot fail and return plain values, and checked_* can fail and returns a Result. Whether method names are camelCase (the standard library's majority) or snake_case is open.

docs.title: 9.3 Stack traces
docs.text: Debug builds produce Python-quality tracebacks (Traceback (most recent call last):, file, line, function, then ExceptionType: message, plus chained causes). Mechanism: frame pointers in debug builds, a deterministic address-to-(function, file, line) table embedded in the binary (sorted by address, so builds stay byte-identical), and the chain of return addresses captured when an exception is thrown and formatted lazily when printed. Release builds omit the tables and the capture. An uncaught exception prints its traceback to stderr and exits with a nonzero status.

docs.title: 9.4 Implementation sketch
docs.text:
• No stack unwinder is required initially. The compiler infers, over the whole program, which functions can throw. A throwing function (one containing an operation that can raise, or calling one that can) returns an extra error value, and each call site checks it and branches. A throw is then an early return, and the compiler already inserts drops on every early exit, so owned values are released correctly and finally is a cleanup block.
  • Callers of functions that cannot throw pay nothing. Because every integer operation can trap, almost every function will be inferred as throwing; the per-call check is the cost. A table-based unwinder (zero happy-path cost, more runtime machinery) is a later optimization. The semantics above do not depend on which implementation is used.
  • A raised exception is a heap-allocated object owned by the in-flight exception and moved into the catch variable, so it depends on Box/owned polymorphism (§2.4) arriving with the object model.

docs.title: 10. Migration notes
docs.text:
Work implied by this design, from the November 2026 audit:

  • Consolidate move/drop logic. Move checking lives in semantic_analyzer.py, again in preprocessor.py (own signature tables, drop insertion), and again in the FIR ownership verifier. Rework this into one source of truth before changing the rules.
  • Fix documentation drift found in the audit: owned this / owned parameters are accepted by the parser although the docs mark the consuming receiver [PLANNED]; fn m(this) on an owned class is silently a read-only borrow; const is documented as enforced but is not; docs write &T in types while the parser takes & before the parameter name; .clone() is [PLANNED] yet FIR has a CloneInst; docs/internal/development/builtin_methods.md is referenced but does not exist.
  • Docs to rewrite once the model ships: docs/reference/memory_management.md (declared authoritative), docs/glossary.md, and the Owned/Copyable mentions in classes.md, functions.md, scoping.md, arrays.md, variables.md, operators.md, type_system.md, overview.md, std/types.md, std/collections.md, std/text.md, the FIR/FLIR internal specs, CLAUDE.md's feature table, and the changelog.
  • Tests: the existing memory tests encode the old model and need an intentional, documented update (per the project's rules on editing tests), plus new coverage for each rule above.

docs.title: 11. Open questions
docs.text:
• Spelling of move (move x vs move(x)) and of the deep-copy hook.
  • Whether & moves into the type position for parameters.
  • Default member visibility and the exact meaning of protected.
  • How Object's common methods are declared and overridden.
  • Whether Option can hold a reference (needed by downcast); whether lossless numeric widening is implicit.
  • Exact std.fs split between Result and thrown IOExceptions; whether a lint should warn on blanket catch (Exception e) by default.
  • Whether and when Box / Shared land relative to capturing closures.

docs.title: 12. Absence: Option<T>, no null [PLANNED]
docs.text:
Decided 2026-11-19.

  • One mechanism. A value that may be absent is an Option<T>. The null literal and the nullable type marker T? are removed from the language. Keeping both would give users two ways to say the same thing.
  • Why Option. It fits the class and library model, composes (it nests, and it can be a generic argument such as ArrayList<Option<T>>), and is unwrapped with match.
  • Explicit, no implicit wrapping. A function declared -> Option<int32> does not accept return 5; or return null;. It returns Some(5) or None(). An implicit wrap would allocate invisibly, make null mean None only in some contexts, and be ambiguous for Option<Option<T>>.
  • Terse through inference. Some(x) and None() infer their type arguments from the expected type (declared return type, typed variable, parameter). Today None() needs the explicit Option<int32>.None() form because a type parameter absent from the arguments cannot be recovered; expected-type inference removes that need without any implicit conversion.
  • Representation. Option<T> becomes a real enum { Some(T), None }, which needs generic enums and match first. Small enums need inline storage (or another compact form) so a maybe-int32 does not allocate.
  • Ordering. Until generic enums land, T?, null and the null-flow rule stay as shipped in 0.6.0. Removal is scheduled with the object model in 0.9.0.
  • Not decided here. An optional-chaining operator and ?-style propagation are deferred; they are tied to operator overloading and the error design (§9.2).

docs.title: language specification and compiler versioning
docs.text: Status: [PLANNED] — a governance and terminology design. Nothing here is implemented: the compiler does not yet read a target spec version, and there is no formal specification document yet (the reference pages under docs/reference are the closest thing, and mix specified behavior with implementation status). The release roadmap is version_planning.md.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
• firescript is the language, and is defined by the firescript Language Specification (fls). When the language is discussed in general, "firescript" means what the fls says.
  • fsc is the firescript Compiler, an implementation of the fls.
  • kiln is the build tool and package manager.
  • The fls and fsc are versioned independently, both with semantic versioning.

All three names are lowercase, like the project name.

docs.title: The compatibility contract
docs.text:
• Every fsc release declares the fls version it implements, for example fsc 2.4.3 implements fls 1.4.3.
  • A project declares the fls version it targets (in its kiln manifest), for example fls = 1.2.5.
  • kiln resolves the newest fsc whose implemented fls version is compatible with the project's target. Under semantic versioning, "compatible" means the same major version and an implemented version greater than or equal to the target: fls 1.4.3 is a superset of fls 1.2.5, so fsc 2.4.3 is chosen for a project targeting fls 1.2.5.
  • A project targeting fls 1.2.5 must not silently depend on later features. fsc therefore has to reject features introduced after the target version (feature gating), including language syntax, semantics, diagnostics that change validity, and standard-library APIs.

docs.title: Current state
docs.text: fsc does not gate features by spec version, and will not until after the self-hosting bootstrap: the gating needs a significant architectural change (every syntactic form, semantic rule, diagnostic, and library API must carry a "since" version and be checked against the target). Until then fsc accepts everything it implements regardless of the target. The work below only prepares for the later change; it adds no gating code.

docs.title: fls
docs.text:
• MAJOR: a change that alters the validity or meaning of a program that was valid under the previous version. That includes removing or renaming a feature, tightening a rule so that formerly accepted programs are rejected, and changing defined behavior.
  • MINOR: backward-compatible additions: new features, new standard-library APIs, new behavior in previously unspecified territory.
  • PATCH: clarifications, corrections of wording or examples, and non-normative changes; no change to which programs are valid or what they do.
  • Before 1.0, per semantic versioning, any 0.x release may make breaking changes.

docs.title: fsc
docs.text: fsc has its own semantic version, which covers the compiler and its tool contract (command line, exit codes, diagnostics format, output layout). A new fsc major is warranted when a tool-contract change breaks users or when support for an fls major version is dropped. Which fls version an fsc release implements is recorded with every release.

docs.title: The beta period (before fls 1.0.0)
docs.text:
• During 0.N, a preliminary fls 1.0.0 is defined and maintained as a draft: the target the project works toward. While it is a draft it carries a pre-release version (working name 1.0.0-draft.N, a semantic-versioning pre-release identifier) and may change freely; the semantic-versioning guarantees above start when fls 1.0.0 is released.
  • fsc 0.N is not guaranteed to be a full implementation of the draft. Each fsc 0.N release states which draft revision it tracks and which parts of it are implemented. The existing status markers ([IMPLEMENTED] / [IN DEVELOPMENT] / [PLANNED]) keep exactly this meaning: they are the implementation status of fsc relative to the draft, and are best generated from the feature registry as an implementation-status table.
  • fls 1.0.0 is released together with fsc 1.0.0, the first release that implements the whole specification and passes the full conformance suite (the self-hosted release). A specification with no passing implementation is only a draft.
  • From then on the versions are independent, as described above.
  • The draft's scope is the feature set the roadmap builds (memory and value model, object model, errors and exceptions, safety rules). Anything the roadmap defers past 1.0 is explicitly out of the draft (for example generic enums, async, macros). Platform targets (Windows, Linux), directives, and the runtime internals are properties of fsc, not of the language, and are not part of the fls.

docs.title: What the specification contains (proposed)
docs.text:
A normative document, using RFC 2119 wording (MUST, SHOULD, MAY), with each feature annotated "since fls X.Y":

  1. Lexical structure (tokens, literals, identifiers, comments, escape sequences)
  2. A formal grammar (EBNF). Today the grammar is implicit in the hand-written parser.
  3. Types (numeric, char, string, arrays, classes, interfaces, generics, nullable types)
  4. Expressions, operators, conversions, and the overflow/trap rules
  5. Statements and control flow
  6. Declarations: functions, classes, interfaces, enums, constants, module-level variables, visibility
  7. The value, copy, move, and borrow model, and const rules
  8. Errors: traps and exceptions, Result
  9. Modules, imports, and exports
  10. Directives and the compilation model (what a conforming implementation must diagnose)
  11. The core library contract: the types the language itself depends on (Object, the primitive bindings, Exception, Result/Option, the standard interfaces)

Decided: the fls contains the core library contract above (the types the language itself depends on). The rest of the standard library is versioned separately from the fls (it may follow its own version or be pinned by kiln), as Java separates the language specification from the platform API.

docs.title: Preparing now, without the architecture change
docs.text:
1. Spec-first changes. A language change is written into the specification (with its "since" version) before or with the compiler change, never only in the compiler.
  2. A machine-readable feature registry derived from the spec: each syntactic form, semantic rule, diagnostic code, and library API with its "since" version. Gating can later be generated from it. Add the registry; do not add gating.
  3. The test suite becomes the conformance suite. Each .fire test records the spec section it covers; the suite is then what any conforming implementation, including the self-hosted fsc, must pass.
  4. Split the changelog into an fls changelog (language and core-library changes, by spec version) and an fsc changelog (compiler and tooling changes).
  5. Status markers keep their meaning. [IMPLEMENTED] / [IN DEVELOPMENT] / [PLANNED] describe the state of fsc relative to the spec. Once a formal spec exists, the spec text carries no status markers; they live in an implementation-status table.
  6. Diagnostic codes are part of the contract. The FS-* codes that identify rule violations should be allocated by the spec (a stable code per specified rule) and stay stable across fsc releases.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• The specification lives in docs/spec/, built up from the existing docs/reference pages.
  • Only the core library contract is part of the fls; the rest of the standard library is versioned separately.
  • Writing the specification itself is deferred: not started until the owner says so. The design decisions it depends on (safety package, exceptions, object model) settle first.
  • The terminology (fls, fsc) is added to CLAUDE.md and used across the docs once the project starts changing the terminology everywhere, not before.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How an fsc that implements several fls major versions (a compatibility mode) is expressed, if that is ever wanted.
  • How the target version interacts with the versions of the separately versioned standard library that kiln pulls.
  • How the existing docs/reference pages are split into normative specification text and the implementation-status table.

docs.title: syscalls docs
docs.text:
Syscalls are only intended to be used in the standard library. When we need them in the standard library, you add this directive at the top of the file:

directive enable_syscalls;

docs.title: Return Type: SyscallResult
docs.text:
All syscalls return a SyscallResult copyable class defined in the standard library:

copyable class SyscallResult {
    status: int32;
    data: string;
}
  • status — An integer status code. 0 or a positive value (e.g. bytes read/written) indicates success. A negative value indicates an error, represented as a negated errno value when available.
  • data — A string containing any output produced by the syscall (e.g. bytes read, environment variable value). Not guaranteed to have a meaningful value — for syscalls that do not produce output (e.g. syscall_write, syscall_close), data will be an empty string.

docs.title: Available Syscalls
docs.text:
Enabling syscalls gives you access to the following functions. Only the basic I/O syscalls are currently implemented; the remaining ones are planned.

Syscall Description status data syscall_open(path, mode) Opens the file at path with the given mode ("r", "w", "a", etc.). Returns a file descriptor. fd (≥ 0) or negative error code empty syscall_read(fd, n) Reads up to n bytes from file descriptor fd. bytes read or negative error code the bytes read as a string syscall_write(fd, buf) Writes string buf to file descriptor fd. bytes written or negative error code empty syscall_close(fd) Closes file descriptor fd. 0 on success or negative error code empty syscall_remove(path) Removes the file at path. 0 on success or negative error code empty syscall_rename(old, new) Renames file old to new. 0 on success or negative error code empty syscall_move(src, dst) Moves file from src to dst (rename first, then copy+remove fallback for cross-device moves). 0 on success or negative error code empty syscall_exec(cmd, args) (planned) Executes command cmd with string[] arguments args. exit code or negative error code empty syscall_getenv(name) (planned) Gets the value of environment variable name. 0 on success or negative error code the variable's value syscall_system(cmd) (planned) Executes shell command cmd via the system shell. exit code or negative error code empty syscall_exit(code) (planned) Exits the process with exit code code. does not return does not return syscall_time() (planned) Returns the current system time as seconds since the Unix epoch. seconds since epoch empty syscall_sleep(ms) (planned) Sleeps for ms milliseconds. 0 on success or negative error code empty

docs.title: How File Descriptors Work
docs.text:
• File descriptors are integers returned in status by syscall_open. Pass them to subsequent read, write, and close calls.
  • Parallel I/O: You can open multiple files at once. Each operation targets a specific file via its descriptor, allowing independent operations on multiple files.
  • Lifetime: The file descriptor remains valid until explicitly closed via syscall_close. After closing, further operations on that descriptor are invalid.
  • Error Handling: status is 0 or positive on success and negative on error.

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
directive enable_syscalls;

open1: SyscallResult = syscall_open("output1.txt", "w");
open2: SyscallResult = syscall_open("output2.txt", "w");

if open1.status >= 0 and open2.status >= 0 {
    syscall_write(open1.status, "foo");
    syscall_write(open2.status, "bar");

    syscall_close(open1.status);
    syscall_close(open2.status);
}

r: SyscallResult = syscall_read(open1.status, 64);
if r.status >= 0 {
    // r.data contains the bytes read
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Syscalls are low-level and intended to be wrapped by higher-level standard library functions (e.g. std.io). Avoid using them directly in user code.
  • syscall_open returns the file descriptor in status, not in data, to keep the integer value directly usable.

docs.title: fuzzing and advanced edge-case testing plan
docs.text: Status: [PLANNED] — nothing here exists yet unless it says so. The release roadmap that schedules this work is version_planning.md. The existing test harness is described in tests/TEST_MANIFEST.md.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• A compiler that never crashes with a Python traceback: every input produces either a binary or a diagnostic.
  • Find bugs that hand-written tests miss, using oracles (a trusted second opinion) instead of hand-written expected output wherever one exists.
  • Keep every found bug permanent: each one becomes a regression test per CLAUDE.md.
  • Stay deterministic: every fuzz run is reproducible from a printed seed (the harness already prints and accepts --seed).

Line coverage is a diagnostic here, not a goal; see the test philosophy in CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: 1.1 Harness integration
docs.text:
• A new fuzz test kind in tests/harness/kinds/, excluded from the default profile so python tests/run.py stays fast; included under --profile full and a scheduled (nightly) CI job. A short fixed-seed smoke run is allowed in the default CI profile.
  • Every failure prints its seed and writes the failing input plus a minimized copy (delta-debugging over tokens/lines) to the work directory.
  • A found bug is fixed, and its minimized repro is added as an ordinary regression test in the feature's category directory. Fuzz targets never get a skip mechanism.
  • Standard library only for generators and mutators (no new dependency) unless a tool is clearly worth it; hypothesis is the one candidate and would be a dev-only dependency.

docs.title: 1.2 Targets
docs.text: Target Input Invariant (oracle) Lexer / parser Mutated corpus of tests/sources/**/*.fire (character, token, and splice mutations) plus grammar-generated programs Never an uncaught Python exception; either diagnostics or success Whole front-end (--check) Same Never crashes; diagnostics have valid locations; same input gives identical diagnostics twice Backend arithmetic Generated well-typed expression programs over every integer/float width Compiled-and-run output equals a Python reference evaluator that implements firescript's wraparound, cast, and shift rules Regex Random patterns and texts within the supported syntax is_match, find_first, find_all, replace agree with Python's re (fullmatch for is_match) on the supported subset; unsupported syntax yields last_error, never a crash ArrayList, HashMap, StringBuilder, split, string methods Random operation sequences Model-based: results equal a Python list / dict / str run through the same operations; no leak or crash Assembler encoder Random instruction/operand combinations Bytes equal GNU as (extends test_asm_encoding.py; see 3.5) FIR / FLIR verifiers Valid FIR/FLIR with one random corruption applied The verifier rejects it with a diagnostic; valid IR from real programs is always accepted Ownership and borrowing (after 0.8.0) Random programs of moves, copies, borrows, scopes, early exits The compiler either rejects with an ownership diagnostic, or the program runs with no use-after-move, leak, or double free

docs.title: 1.3 Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A runtime allocation counter (debug-only, behind a directive) so leaks and double frees are detectable at run time and not only by the static heap verifier.
  • A small generator library under tests/support/ (typed expression generator, program generator, pattern generator) shared by the fuzz targets.
  • Ownership fuzzing waits for the 0.8.0 memory model, since the rules change; the other targets can start now.

docs.title: 2. Advanced edge-case testing
docs.text:
Systematic matrices for places where bugs hide, written as ordinary run tests (or generated into them):

  • Numeric boundaries. For every integer width: min, max, ±1, overflow wraparound for + - *, MIN / -1, division and modulo by zero behavior, shifts by amounts at and beyond the width, every cast pair. Floats: NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, denormals, float-to-int out of range, parsing and printing round trips. float128 against published IEEE binary128 test vectors.
  • Strings and arrays. Empty, very long, embedded escapes, non-ASCII bytes; boundary indices for substring, indexOf, negative array indexing, zero-length arrays, out-of-range access (define and test the behavior).
  • Compiler robustness. Deeply nested expressions and blocks (the parser is recursive; a deep nest must give a diagnostic, not a Python RecursionError), very long identifiers and literals, many functions, very large files.
  • Stack and heap stress. Deep recursion limits, allocate/free churn over many iterations with owned elements (ArrayList, HashMap, strings, classes), large arrays.
  • Feature interaction matrix. Pairwise combinations of generics, ownership, nullable types, classes, generators, enums/match, and imports (generated, so the matrix stays maintainable).
  • Error-code coverage. Every diagnostic code the compiler can emit, and every verifier check, has at least one test that triggers it. Checkable mechanically by listing the codes in firescript/errors.py and the verifiers against the test annotations.
  • Metamorphic tests. Semantics-preserving rewrites must not change output: rename identifiers, reorder independent top-level definitions, add redundant parentheses or blocks, insert dead code, split expressions into temporaries.
  • Determinism variations. Extend the existing compile-twice check to vary PYTHONHASHSEED, the working directory, and path spelling, since the compiler must never depend on hash order.
  • Cross-target (after Linux support): the same source produces the same output on both targets.

docs.title: 3. Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Start with what needs no new infrastructure: error-code coverage check, PYTHONHASHSEED determinism variation, numeric-boundary matrices, and the regex and collection oracles.
  2. Then the fuzz kind and the corpus-mutation parser fuzzer, with minimization.
  3. Then the generated-program backend differential (arithmetic and casts).
  4. Then the allocation counter, which unlocks leak detection for the stdlib model tests and later the ownership fuzzer.
  5. tests/python/backend/test_asm_encoding.py currently compares against a MinGW as that produces COFF; on Linux as produces ELF, so its cases fail locally. Reading .text from ELF as well as COFF would make that test usable on both and is a good first step for the encoder fuzzer.
  6. When the self-hosted front-end and backend exist (0.11.0 and 0.12.0), the Python and firescript compilers become oracles for each other: fuzz both with the same inputs and require identical diagnostics, FIR, and bytes.

docs.title: 4. Release hooks
docs.text: Scheduling is in version_planning.md: infrastructure and the no-dependency items alongside cross-target testing in 0.7.0, the ownership fuzzer in 0.8.0, dispatch/interface/binding generation in 0.9.0, the two-compiler differential in 0.11.0 and 0.12.0, and "no open crashers from a nightly fuzz run" as a 1.0.0 release criterion.

docs.title: firescript version planning
docs.text:
Planning for future versions toward 1.0.0 — Titan, the self-hosted release.

Terminology. The language is defined by the firescript Language Specification (fls); the compiler is the firescript Compiler (fsc). They are versioned independently — see spec_and_versioning.md. During 0.N the roadmap below builds toward a preliminary fls 1.0.0; fsc 0.N tracks that draft without being a full implementation. fls 1.0.0 and fsc 1.0.0 are released together when the compiler implements the whole specification.

docs.title: Guiding Vision
docs.text:
The goal of firescript 1.0 is a self-hosted compiler: a firescript compiler written in firescript that can compile itself. Every version from 0.6.0 onward builds explicitly toward this end state.

The bootstrap path has three phases: 1. Stdlib foundation — give firescript the data structures and string utilities a compiler needs (ArrayList, HashMap, StringBuilder, enums, pattern matching) 2. Language maturity — a value-semantics memory model, const and visibility, an interface- based object model, diagnostics infrastructure — so the firescript compiler code is clean and idiomatic. This precedes self-hosting so the compiler is not written twice. Linux support (Python backend) is pulled forward ahead of it. 3. Self-hosted implementation — write the compiler front-end, then the backend, in firescript, culminating in a full bootstrap

docs.title: Working in tasks
docs.text: Work is done as small, self-contained tasks, one per session. A task block (below, under each release) carries everything a fresh session needs, so nothing depends on chat history. A session reads CLAUDE.md, this section, its one task block, and the docs the block links to, and does nothing else.

docs.title: Session protocol
docs.text:
1. Pick one task whose dependencies are done (the owner usually names it). Set its status to in-progress with the branch name.
  2. Work in the main checkout on a branch task/T-xxx-nn (or continue the named WIP branch). No subagent fan-out and no parallel agents: one task, one session, one line of work.
  3. Keep runs small. Use targeted tests (python tests/run.py <path> --no-coverage) while working. Run the full CI profile only once, at the end: python tests/run.py --profile ci (about 10 minutes; it also checks determinism on every run test).
  4. Linux needs the wine environment (the native backend targets Windows only): export FIRESCRIPT_TEST_TARGET=windows/x86_64 FIRESCRIPT_TEST_RUN_PREFIX=wine WINEDEBUG=-all (see "Running on Linux" in tests/TEST_MANIFEST.md).
  5. Follow CLAUDE.md: regression test with every bug fix, changelog entry with every user-facing change, manifest and status-marker updates in the same commit, one logical change per commit, determinism, never skip a test, never change an expectation just to pass.
  6. Tests must be portable to Windows: no assertions on OS-specific error wording, no characters invalid in Windows file names (<>:"\|?*) in test ids or paths, never rely on the platform default text encoding (always pass encoding="utf-8"). Windows CI is the real check.
  7. If a task grows, stop and split it. Add the new smaller tasks to this file, finish only the first, and say so. A task that needs more than one session was defined too big.
  8. Finish: merge to main, set the status to done with the commit, and note anything the next task needs. Push only when the owner says so (the project settings allow git push origin main).
  9. Record decisions here, not in chat. An owner decision goes into the task block or the relevant design doc in the same commit.

Status values: todo, in-progress (branch), done (commit), blocked (reason). Sizes: S is a short session, M is one full session. There is no L: split it.

docs.title: Decisions that apply to every task
docs.text:
Confirmed by the owner. Design detail is in language_model_redesign.md; the audit evidence is in test_audit/README.md.

  • Safety is the model. Integer overflow, division by zero, MIN / -1, out-of-range array indexing, and float-to-int casts of NaN/infinity/out-of-range values trap (a runtime error; catchable exceptions come in 0.9.0). Narrowing as casts between integer widths stay explicit truncation. Explicit wrapping/saturating/checked operations exist for control.
  • Braces are required on if, else, while, for. Missing return on a path in a non-void function is an error. Unknown string/char escapes are errors. A nullable value may not flow into a non-nullable position (the minimal null-check narrowing rule is a judgment call to review).
  • Explicit receivers are required. Instance methods declare &this or &mut this; constructors declare &mut this; consuming receivers on ordinary methods are not supported yet. this (the binding) can never be assigned; the receiver governs mutation of the object.
  • const cannot be reassigned. const class fields are [PLANNED].
  • Constraint unions are written Union<A, B> (replacing A | B); Intersection<A, B> is [PLANNED]; & is a syntax error; unknown constraint names are errors.
  • The legacy conversion builtins are removed (toInt, toFloat, toDouble, toBool, toChar, toString, int, i32_to_f64, i32_to_f32, f64_to_i32, f32_to_i32, i32_to_str, i64_to_str, f64_to_str, f32_to_str). as casts stay until the 0.9.0 bindings.
  • Absence is Option<T>; null and T? go away (decided 2026-11-19). One mechanism, not two. Option<T> stays explicit: no implicit wrapping of a value or null into an Option on return or assignment. Some(5) / None() infer their type arguments from the expected type (a declared return type, a typed variable, a parameter), so Option<int32>.None() need not be spelled out there. T?, the null literal and the null-flow rule are removed once generic enums and match exist (0.9.0); until then they stay as shipped in 0.6.0, and the narrowing rule under T-060-04 is interim. Design: language_model_redesign.md §12.
  • Errors (0.9.0): operations throw catchable exceptions (Exception extends Object); fallible function calls return Result. Until then traps print a message and exit through one runtime entry point.
  • No real users yet: breaking changes need only a changelog Breaking Changes entry.
  • Deferred past 0.6.0: borrow-checker holes and diagnostic-cascade cleanup (0.8.0 memory rework), the fls/fsc terminology work, the formal specification, fuzzing.
  • Open owner decisions (do not decide in a task): a ?-style propagation operator; Result.unwrap() throwing; an Indexable interface for list[i]; naming of the explicit arithmetic functions (camelCase vs snake_case); whether catch can rethrow; the std.fs split between Result and exceptions.
  • 0.6.0 is done when every task below is done, the full CI profile passes locally, the Windows CI run is green, and the owner has cut the release (moving changelog entries into the versioned section is the owner's job).

docs.title: 0.6.0 — Griffin (Current)
docs.text:
Theme: Standard library foundations for compiler writing.

The firescript compiler needs rich collections and string utilities that are simply not expressible with fixed-size arrays alone. This release fills those gaps so the subsequent self-hosting work is not blocked by missing data structures.

docs.title: Language features
docs.text: Feature Rationale enum / sum types with data payloads AST node types, tokens, and type variants map naturally to enums. Without them the compiler code is class hierarchies and manual dispatch. match expressions Ergonomic destructuring of enums. Without match, working with enums is verbose if-else chains. ArrayList<T> in @firescript/std.collections Dynamic arrays are the single most critical missing collection — needed for token lists, AST child lists, symbol tables, etc. HashMap<K,V> in @firescript/std.collections Symbol tables, type environments, and identifier lookups require associative maps. StringBuilder in @firescript/std.text Code generation and error message formatting need efficient string accumulation. Extended string methods: split, substring, indexOf, startsWith, endsWith, trim, lower, upper, replace Lexing and string processing require these — cannot write a parser without substring search and splitting. Result<T,E> proper error type Compiler phases propagate errors; a well-typed Result is essential for ergonomic error handling in firescript code.

docs.title: Standard library
docs.text:
• New module @firescript/std.collections — ArrayList<T>, HashMap<K,V> (and later Stack<T>, Queue<T>, Deque<T>)
  • ArrayList<T> — done: add/removeLast/get/set/size, capacity-doubling growth, correct for both Copyable and Owned element types (owned elements are dropped by the generated destructor before the backing buffer is freed — see the new @owns_elements class decorator in flir/lowering.py). Built on two new compiler intrinsics private to std/collections/, fs_rt_array_new<T>/fs_rt_array_copy<T>, which allocate/copy a T[] buffer of a runtime-determined element count (the "Dynamic arrays (stdlib)" CLAUDE.md feature-table entry, now flipped to [IMPLEMENTED]).
  • enumerate generator for iterating over ArrayList<T> with index/value pairs Pair<int32,T> — done. Surfaced (and fixed) a compiler bug where a generic-class-shaped type string with an unresolved nested type argument (e.g. Pair<int32, T>) substituted the outer type but never the type parameters inside it, and a second bug where generic generator functions had no type-argument inference/monomorphization at all.
  • HashMap<K,V> — done: set/get/has/remove/length/size, open addressing with tombstones, capacity-doubling growth at a 70% load factor. K restricted to a fixed hashable set (integer types, bool, char, string) via a new fs_rt_hash<K> compiler intrinsic (dispatched by concrete K at FLIR-lowering time, same pattern as fs_rt_array_new<T>) — no Hashable trait to dispatch through generically until the interfaces release (0.9.0). get/remove return V directly rather than Option<V> — not because of a compiler gap any more (see below), just to keep this milestone's changes scoped; switching to Option<V> is a viable, purely additive follow-up. Surfaced (and fixed) three more previously-unexercised generic-class bugs: a later type-checking pass only pushed a method's own (empty) type parameters into scope, clobbering the enclosing class's type parameters for the whole method body, so comparing two values of the class's own type parameter with == failed; a generic class method calling another method on the same instance didn't monomorphize the callee correctly (method receivers are always typed by bare class name, never ClassName<Args>, and lowering assumed otherwise); and drop() on a bare generic-type-parameter value that turns out concretely Copyable/primitive tried to heap-free its raw bit pattern instead of no-op'ing (needed for HashMap<K,V>.set()'s conditional drop(key) on overwrite). Also led directly into full nullable-scalar support (locals, class fields, function/method/constructor parameters, and plain-function return types all now carry a real "has a value" tag, not just a zero-lowered null) — see the changelog and Option<T>/CopyableOption<T> note below.
  • Nullable-scalar types (int32?, bool?, char?, and the other fixed-width numeric types) — done: a real, separate "has a value" tag alongside the value itself (a companion bool binding/field/parameter, added transparently by the compiler), so null and a legitimate stored 0/false are always distinguishable. Covers local variables, class fields, function/method/constructor parameters, and (for plain functions) return types (fn foo() -> int32?, previously a hard parse error — lifted this milestone). A nullable-scalar return is compiled to an internal __NullableReturn<T> struct return, unwrapped transparently at the call site (evaluating the callee at most once, even when both its value and has-value flag are needed). Option<T>/CopyableOption<T> needed zero source changes to become correct for a primitive T — Option<int32>(0).isSome() now correctly returns true. String/class/array nullables were already unambiguous via the pointer value 0 and are untouched by this.
  • New module @firescript/std.text — StringBuilder — done: backed by an ArrayList<string> of fragments rather than a raw growable byte buffer (std/internal/strings.fire can't construct an ArrayList<T> itself — internal runtime files carry no import statements), with append/length/build. build() drains fragments with ArrayList<T>.removeLast(), not get()/enumerate() (unsafe for the Owned string element type — see docs/reference/std/collections.md). No zero-arg constructor (StringBuilder("") starts empty instead) — see the compiler-improvements note below.
  • Extended string methods — done: .indexOf(), .substring(), .startsWith(), .endsWith(), .trim(), .replace(), alongside the existing .length()/.upper()/ .lower(), all via @builtin_method in std/internal/strings.fire (.indexOf()/ .substring() decorate the pre-existing fs_rt_str_index_of/fs_rt_str_slice primitives directly). split is the one method from this list that's a plain function (split(s, delim)), not a .split() dot-method — it needs to return ArrayList<string>, and @builtin_method backing functions live in std/internal/, which (as above) can't reference ArrayList<T>. Lives in @firescript/std.text alongside StringBuilder.
  • Enhanced @firescript/std.types — Result<T,E>/CopyableResult<T,E> — done: value: T?/error: E? fields (mirrors Option<T>'s pattern exactly, including automatic nullable-scalar correctness for a primitive T/E), isOk()/isErr(). No Ok/Err static factory constructors and no combinators (map, unwrapOr, etc.) — while probing the natural Result.Ok(value)/Result.Err(error) design, discovered static methods on generic classes didn't work in any form at the time (explicit type arguments, Box<int32>.make(5), were a parser error; inferred type arguments, Box.make(5), crashed AST->FIR conversion). Result/CopyableResult are constructed directly instead (Result<T,E>(value, error), null on the unused side); the underlying compiler gap is now fixed (see generics/generic_class_static_method_inferred.fire and generic_class_static_method_explicit.fire under Compiler improvements below) but Result was kept as direct construction rather than revisited, as adding Ok/Err factories now would be a purely additive follow-up with no functional need.
  • @firescript/std.regex — full regex matching engine (lexer, parser, NFA/DFA compilation, matching over strings). Required by FCL and by compiler string-processing needs. (Existing stub needs real implementation.)
  • Parser + backtracking matcher over a compiled program (literals, escapes, ., anchors, groups, alternation, * + ?, classes) — done
  • Shorthand classes \d \D \w \W \s \S, counted quantifiers {n}/{n,}/{n,m}, non-capturing groups — done
  • Capture groups with submatch extraction (Match, find_first, find_all, replace with $0..$9) — done
  • NFA/DFA compilation (linear-time matching), lookarounds, non-greedy quantifiers, backreferences, named groups, \b — not done

docs.title: Compiler improvements
docs.text:
• Support enum and match in the front-end pipeline (lexer, parser, semantic analysis, FIR lowering) — done: enum declarations (tag-only and named data-payload variants, positional construction) and match expressions (name-based payload binding with optional rename, exhaustiveness/duplicate/wildcard-order checks, statement and value-producing forms, tag-dispatched destructors for owned payload data) work across the full pipeline. Generic enums (enum Option<T>) remain a follow-up.
  • Support ArrayList<T>, HashMap<K,V>, StringBuilder, and Result<T,E> as stdlib modules with appropriate compiler intrinsics where needed — ArrayList<T> (including enumerate), HashMap<K,V>, and Result<T,E>/CopyableResult<T,E> done; also unblocked unsized array class fields (previously rejected entirely), added a fs_rt_hash<K> intrinsic and multi-field @owns_elements support, and fixed a series of narrow, previously-unexercised generic-class/generator bugs both surfaced (method-call return-type substitution for a bare type-parameter return, missing receiver on a method with no explicit &this/this destroying the object on every call, a generic class's own bare-name Owned/Copyable registration, a generator-loop-variable drop gap for Owned yield types, nested-type-argument substitution inside a compound generic type string, generic generator functions having no type-argument inference/monomorphization at all, class-body type-parameter scoping in the standalone type-checking pass, a generic method calling another method on the same instance, drop() on a primitive corrupting the heap, and null for a nullable scalar type) — see docs/changelog.md's 0.6.0 Bug Fixes. Another one surfaced while designing Result<T,E> and later fixed: static methods on generic classes didn't work in any call form. The parser's Type.method(...) special case (and its Identifier<TypeArgs>.method(...) counterpart) only ever recognized a concrete class name, since a generic class's bare template name is deliberately absent from self.user_types/self.user_methods (registered as a generic_class_templates entry instead); type_system.py's TYPE_METHOD_CALL validation and ast_to_fir.py's monomorphization needed the equivalent generic-template fallback a constructor call already had, plus type-argument inference from the call's own arguments (there's no receiver instance to read concrete type arguments from) for the no-explicit-type-args form — see generics/generic_class_static_method_inferred.fire and generic_class_static_method_explicit.fire. Separately, fixed an unrelated lexer bug hit while writing Result<T,E>'s regression tests: identifiers with true/false/null as a literal prefix (e.g. false_ok) failed to parse, since those three literal token patterns (unlike every keyword) had no trailing word-boundary — see docs/changelog.md's 0.6.0 Bug Fixes and tests/sources/identifiers/.
  • Extended string methods and StringBuilder/split done — see the Standard library section above. Fixed another real bug hit while building StringBuilder: an owned value moved via a method call through a field-access receiver (this.parts.add(s)) was never recognized as moved, so it was also auto-dropped at scope exit (FIRV-O2) — semantic_analyzer.py and preprocessor.py each only resolved a receiver's type for a bare-identifier receiver, and the generic-field case additionally needed the "strip generic type arguments" normalization ast_to_fir.py already had — see docs/changelog.md's 0.6.0 Bug Fixes and tests/sources/memory/memory_field_receiver_method_move.fire. Two more surfaced in the same investigation, and were also fixed (all tests/sources/known_issues/ entries from this release are now resolved, with regression tests moved to their normal categories): a same-file class's bare Foo(args) constructor call resolved against field order instead of the real declared constructor whenever they diverged (func_name in self.user_types in parser/type_system.py now checks self.user_methods for a real constructor first — see classes/classes_zero_arg_constructor_bare_call.fire), and a class imported from another module lost its type for raw field access (not method calls) after a bare-call construction (the deferred-import suppression in FIELD_ACCESS handling widened from composite-generic-only to any not-yet-resolved non-primitive type — see classes/classes_cross_module_bare_construct_field_access.fire).
  • Added Some/None/Ok/Err static factories and unwrapOr() to Option/CopyableOption/Result/CopyableResult done — see docs/reference/std/types.md. Building these surfaced four more previously-unexercised compiler bugs, all fixed (see docs/changelog.md's 0.6.0 Bug Fixes): the FLIR verifier's store check was the one place not using the codebase's established pointer-leniency comparison, breaking this.value = null; for a pointer-shaped generic field; the same assignment for a scalar-shaped generic field lowered null to a bare pointer instead of the scalar's zero value, since the assignment-conversion paths never propagated the target's expected type before converting a null RHS; a generic class referencing itself inside its own body (a static factory returning Box<T>, or a self-call like this.isSome() from another of its own methods) failed to parse/type-check in a file with no imports at all — exactly std/types/init.fire's own shape — because the enclosing class isn't registered in the parser's normal registries until its whole body finishes parsing, and a pre-existing fallback for this only ever activated in files that happened to have an unrelated import; fixed with a dedicated _current_generic_class_name tracked independently across the parser's parse-time and separate type-check-time traversals. And a general, non-generic-specific gap: a bare (no explicit type arguments) type-qualified static call on a class imported from another module (Counter.fromDouble(5)) had no deferred-import parsing fallback at all — only the <TypeArgs> form did — so it silently fell through to being parsed as an ordinary instance method call and crashed AST->FIR conversion.
  • Implement @firescript/std.regex with necessary runtime support
  • Regenerate and freeze goldens for all new features

• Goal: Windows CI is fully green.

After the compiler started reading source as UTF-8 (6c0bb25), the likely cause is the test harness reading each test file (the /* EXPECT */ block, directives) with the platform default encoding (cp1252 on Windows).
  • Steps: find every open( without encoding= in tests/harness/ (expectations, discovery, directives, workdir) and read as UTF-8; add a Python test that forces a non-UTF-8 default (LC_ALL=C PYTHONUTF8=0 PYTHONCOERCECLOCALE=0, as in tests/python/cli/test_main_arg_errors.py) and parses a non-ASCII EXPECT block; push and check the Windows run.
