import @firescript/std.types.Pair;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

v: ArrayList<int32> = ArrayList<int32>();
v.add(10);
v.add(20);
v.add(30);

for (pair: Pair<int32, int32> in enumerate(v)) {
    println(pair.first);   // index
    println(pair.second);  // value
}

docs.title: HashMap<K,V>
docs.text:
class HashMap<K, V> {
    fn HashMap(&mut this);

    fn size(&this) -> int32;

    fn set(&mut this, key: K, value: V);
    fn has(&this, key: K) -> bool;
    fn get(&mut this, key: K) -> V;
    fn remove(&mut this, key: K) -> V;
}

An open-addressing hash table with linear probing and tombstones, growing (capacity doubles, starting at 8) when the load factor crosses 70%.

Example:

import @firescript/std.collections.HashMap;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

ages: HashMap<string, int32> = HashMap<string, int32>();
ages.set("Alice", 30);
ages.set("Bob", 25);
println(ages.size());        // 2
println(ages.has("Alice"));    // true
println(ages.get("Alice"));    // 30

ages.set("Alice", 31);         // overwrite
println(ages.get("Alice"));    // 31

removed: int32 = ages.remove("Bob");
println(removed);              // 25
println(ages.has("Bob"));      // false

Methods:

  • size(): Number of entries currently stored.
  • set(key, value): Inserts or overwrites the entry for key.
  • has(key): Returns whether key is present.
  • get(key) / remove(key): Only well-defined when has(key) is true first -- like core array indexing (and ArrayList<T>.get()), there's no presence check. Calling either for an absent key reads whatever currently occupies the slot probing would have chosen for an insert, which for a removed slot can be a stale, already-moved-out pointer for an Owned V. Always check has() first.
  • remove(key) moves the stored value out and marks the slot a tombstone in the same operation, so it's safe to call for any V (Owned or Copyable) -- matching ArrayList<T>.removeLast()'s equivalent safety argument.
  • get(key) reads the value out without removing it, so (like ArrayList<T>.get()) it's only safe for Copyable-ish V (numeric types, bool, char) -- for an Owned V the returned copy and the map's own copy would alias the same allocation.

docs.title: Key type restrictions
docs.text: HashMap<K,V> is restricted to a fixed hashable key set: integer types (int8..uint64), bool, char, and string. firescript has no Hashable trait to dispatch hashing through generically yet (planned for a future release alongside Owned/Copyable generic constraints; see docs/internal/version_planning.md's 0.7.0 "Wyvern" milestone). Instantiating HashMap<K,V> with any other K and then actually using it (set/get/ has/remove) is a compile-time error, not a silent miscompile.

docs.title: Why no Option<V> for "not found"?
docs.text: get()/remove() return V directly rather than Option<V> -- use has() first (or, for remove(), rely on it being safe to call unconditionally; see above). This is no longer a representation-gap workaround: nullable scalar types now carry a real "has a value" tag (see docs/changelog.md's 0.6.0 entry), so Option<V>(null) vs. Option<V>(value) is correctly distinguishable for any V, including primitives. Switching get()/remove() to return Option<V> is a viable, purely additive follow-up (it doesn't need any further compiler work) -- it just hasn't been done in this release, to keep this change scoped to the compiler-level fix.

docs.title: Usage Notes
docs.text:
• ArrayList<T>/HashMap<K,V> are built on compiler intrinsics private to std/collections/: fs_rt_array_new<T>/fs_rt_array_copy<T> allocate/copy a T[] buffer of a runtime-determined element count (ordinary fixed-size arrays can only be sized by a compile-time literal), and fs_rt_hash<K> computes a key's hash, dispatched by concrete K at compile time. These are not user-facing API.
  • Stack<T>, Queue<T>, and Deque<T> are planned follow-ups (see docs/internal/version_planning.md's 0.6.0 "Griffin" milestone) -- not yet implemented.

docs.title: File System (std.fs)
docs.text: The std.fs module provides file-system operations through an object-oriented File API centered on methods and result types.

docs.title: File
docs.text:
Represents a file path and provides methods for common file operations.

class File {
    path: string;

    fn File(&mut this, path: string);

    fn read(&this) -> FileResult;
    fn readBytes(&this, bytes: int32) -> FileResult;
    fn writeAll(&this, data: string) -> FileResult;
    fn appendAll(&this, data: string) -> FileResult;
    fn exists(&this) -> bool;
    fn remove(&this) -> FileResult;
    fn renameTo(&mut this, new_path: string) -> FileResult;
    fn moveTo(&mut this, dst_path: string) -> FileResult;
}

Constructor:

fn File(&mut this, path: string)

Create a File instance for the given path. The path is stored but the file is not opened until an operation is called.

Parameters: - path: File path (relative or absolute)

Example:

import @firescript/std.fs.File;

myFile: File = File("hello.txt");

docs.title: FileResult
docs.text:
Encapsulates the result of a file operation.

class FileResult {
    status: int32;
    data: string;

    fn FileResult(status: int32, data: string);

    fn ok(&this) -> bool;
    fn err_code(&this) -> int32;
    fn result_status(&this) -> int32;
    fn result_data(&this) -> string;
}

Fields: - status: Operation status (≥ 0 for success, negative errno for failure) - data: Operation output (e.g., file contents for reads), empty for most writes

Check the status: A negative status indicates an error. Use FileResult methods to inspect results.

docs.title: read()
docs.text:
fn read(&this) -> FileResult

Read the entire file contents into a string.

Returns: FileResult with status = bytes read (on success) or negative error code

Example:

import @firescript/std.fs.File;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

f: File = File("data.txt");
r: FileResult = f.read();
if (r.ok()) {
    println(r.result_data());
}

docs.title: readBytes(bytes: int32)
docs.text:
fn readBytes(&this, bytes: int32) -> FileResult

Read up to the specified number of bytes.

Parameters: - bytes: Maximum bytes to read

Returns: FileResult with status = bytes actually read

Example:

chunk: FileResult = f.readBytes(1024);

docs.title: writeAll(data: string)
docs.text:
fn writeAll(&this, data: string) -> FileResult

Write data to the file, overwriting if it exists.

Parameters: - data: String data to write

Returns: FileResult with status = bytes written (on success) or error code

Example:

w: FileResult = f.writeAll("Hello!");

docs.title: appendAll(data: string)
docs.text:
fn appendAll(&this, data: string) -> FileResult

Append data to the end of the file.

Parameters: - data: String data to append

Returns: FileResult with status = bytes written (on success) or error code

Example:

a: FileResult = f.appendAll("\nMore text");

docs.title: exists()
docs.text:
fn exists(&this) -> bool

Check if the file exists and is readable.

Returns: true if file exists and can be opened for reading, false otherwise

Example:

if (f.exists()) {
    println("File found!");
}

docs.title: remove()
docs.text:
fn remove(&this) -> FileResult

Delete the file.

Returns: FileResult with status = 0 on success, negative error code on failure

Example:

f.remove();

docs.title: renameTo(new_path: string)
docs.text:
fn renameTo(&mut this, new_path: string) -> FileResult

Rename (or move within same filesystem) to a new path. Updates the File path on success.

Parameters: - new_path: New file path

Returns: FileResult with status = 0 on success

Example:

f.renameTo("newname.txt");

docs.title: moveTo(dst_path: string)
docs.text:
fn moveTo(&mut this, dst_path: string) -> FileResult

Move file to a new location with cross-filesystem fallback. On cross-device moves, automatically falls back to copy + delete. Updates the File path on success.

Parameters: - dst_path: Destination path

Returns: FileResult with status = 0 on success

Example:

f.moveTo("/other/location/file.txt");

docs.title: ok()
docs.text:
fn ok(&this) -> bool

Check if operation succeeded (status >= 0).

Example:

if (result.ok()) {
    println("Success!");
}

docs.title: err_code()
docs.text:
fn err_code(&this) -> int32

Extract the error code (positive errno value). Returns 0 if operation succeeded.

Example:

err: int32 = result.err_code();
if (err > 0) {
    println("Error: " + (err as string));
}

docs.title: result_status()
docs.text:
fn result_status(&this) -> int32

Get the raw status field (positive on success, negative errno on failure).

docs.title: result_data()
docs.text:
fn result_data(&this) -> string

Get the data field (file contents for reads, empty for writes).

docs.title: Error Codes
docs.text:
File operations return negative errno values on error:

  • -2: ENOENT (file not found)
  • -13: EACCES (permission denied)
  • -28: ENOSPC (no space on device)
  • -30: EROFS (read-only filesystem)
  • etc.

Consult your system's errno.h for a complete list.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import @firescript/std.fs.File;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

config: File = File("config.txt");

// Write
write_result: FileResult = config.writeAll("setting=value");
if (write_result.ok()) {
    println("Configuration saved");
}

// Read
read_result: FileResult = config.read();
if (read_result.ok()) {
    println("Configuration: " + read_result.result_data());
}

// Cleanup
config.remove();

docs.title: Standard I/O (std.io)
docs.text: The std.io module provides basic output utilities for printing values to standard output.

docs.title: print
docs.text:
void print<T>(&T value)

Print a value to standard output without a trailing newline. The value is implicitly converted to a string.

Parameters: - value: Any type (will be converted to string for output)

Example:

import @firescript/std.io.print;

print("Hello");
print(42);
print(3.14);

docs.title: println
docs.text:
void println<T>(&T value)

Print a value to standard output followed by a newline.

Parameters: - value: Any type (will be converted to string for output)

Example:

import @firescript/std.io.println;

println("Hello, World!");
println(100);

docs.title: Supported Types
docs.text:
Both print and println are generic and support all built-in types that can be converted to strings:

  • Numeric types (intN, uintN, floatN)
  • bool
  • char
  • string

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Both functions are generic and polymorphic; they infer the type from the argument.
  • Output goes directly to standard output (stdout).

docs.title: Math (std.math)
docs.text:
The std.math module provides basic mathematical utilities.

Status: abs, min, max, and clamp are exported and importable today. The module also contains trigonometry, sqrt, pow, angle-conversion helpers, and a large set of mathematical constants, but those are not yet exported and cannot be imported from user code — they are listed at the bottom of this page as [IN DEVELOPMENT].

docs.title: Numeric Constraint
docs.text:
The exported functions are generic over the Numeric constraint, a type union covering all integer and floating-point types:

Numeric = int8 | int16 | int32 | int64 | uint8 | uint16 | uint32 | uint64 | float32 | float64 | float128

Because the functions are generic, all arguments in a call must share the same type.

docs.title: abs(x: T, zero: T)
docs.text:
Return the absolute value of x. The second argument supplies the zero value for the type (e.g., 0 for int32, 0.0 for float64).

import @firescript/std.math.abs;

v: int32 = abs(-42, 0);           // 42
f: float64 = abs(-3.14, 0.0);     // 3.14

docs.title: min(a: T, b: T)
docs.text:
Return the smaller of two values.

import @firescript/std.math.min;

result: int32 = min(5, 3);        // 3

docs.title: max(a: T, b: T)
docs.text:
Return the larger of two values.

import @firescript/std.math.max;

result: int32 = max(5, 3);        // 5

docs.title: clamp(x: T, lo: T, hi: T)
docs.text:
Constrain x to the range [lo, hi].

import @firescript/std.math.clamp;

result: int32 = clamp(10, 0, 5);  // 5

You can also import several symbols at once:

import @firescript/std.math.{max, min, abs, clamp}

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import @firescript/std.math.{max, min, clamp};
import @firescript/std.io.println;

biggest: int32 = max(3, 7);
smallest: float64 = min(2.5, 1.5);
bounded: int32 = clamp(15, 0, 10);

println(biggest);   // 7
println(smallest);  // 1.5
println(bounded);   // 10

Note: assign the result of a generic call to a variable before passing it to another generic function (like println). Nesting generic calls directly (e.g., println(max(3, 7))) currently fails to compile — a known limitation.

docs.title: Not Yet Exported [IN DEVELOPMENT]
docs.text:
The following exist in the module sources but are private (not exported), so they cannot be imported yet:

  • Functions (firescript/std/math/init.fire): sqrt, pow, pow_int, sin, cos, tan, lerp, deg_to_rad, rad_to_deg
  • Constants (firescript/std/math/constants.fire): precision-specific constants for pi (PI32/PI64/PI128, plus PI_2_*, PI_4_*, INV_PI*, SQRT_PI*, LN_PI*), Euler's number (E*, LOG2_E*, LOG10_E*), natural logs (LN_2_*, LN_10_*), square roots (SQRT_2_*, SQRT_3_*, SQRT_1_2_*), special constants (EULER_GAMMA*, PHI*, CATALAN*), and degree/radian conversion multipliers (DEG_TO_RAD*, RAD_TO_DEG*)

These will be documented here once they are exported and tested.

docs.title: Standard Library Overview
docs.text: firescript includes a standard library under the @firescript/std namespace, providing utilities for common programming tasks.

docs.title: Guide to Modules
docs.text:
• I/O: Formatted output with print and println
  • File System: File operations via the File class and FileResult helpers
  • Math: Mathematical functions
  • Regex: Regular-expression matching, anchors, and pattern validation
  • Command-Line Arguments: Argument parsing for CLI programs
  • Types: Generic container types (Pair, Option, Result)
  • Collections: Dynamically-growable arrays and hash tables (ArrayList<T>, HashMap<K,V>)
  • Text: String accumulation and splitting (StringBuilder, split)
  • Ranges: range, rangeFrom, and rangeStep generators for counting loops (@firescript/std.ranges)
  • FCL Lexer: Lexer for parsing firescript config language (FCL) data (@firescript/std.fcl)

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
Standard library modules are imported using @firescript/std namespace syntax:

import @firescript/std.io.println;
import @firescript/std.fs.File;
import @firescript/std.math.max;
import @firescript/std.fcl.next_token;  // FCL lexer

You can also import at the module level:

import @firescript/std.io;  // imports all I/O exports
import @firescript/std.fcl;  // imports all FCL lexer functions

Or use wildcard imports:

import @firescript/std.types.*;  // imports Pair, Option, etc.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: Most file-system operations return result types (e.g., FileResult) that encode success/failure in a status field. Check the File System module for details on error semantics and FileResult methods like ok().

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Prefer stdlib over syscalls: User code should use standard library modules, not low-level syscalls (which require directive enable_syscalls).
  • Explicit imports: Import specific symbols to avoid namespace pollution and make dependencies clear.
  • Check result status: Always inspect result types after file operations to handle errors robustly.

docs.title: std.regex
docs.text:
@firescript/std.regex provides a pure firescript regular-expression module: matching, position-aware matching, capture groups, search helpers, and replacement.

Status: everything below marked [IMPLEMENTED] is complete and covered by tests under tests/sources/std/regex/. Items marked [PLANNED] do not work yet.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import @firescript/std.io.println;
import @firescript/std.regex.is_match;
import @firescript/std.regex.find_at;
import @firescript/std.regex.find_first;
import @firescript/std.regex.replace;
import @firescript/std.regex.last_error;
import @firescript/std.regex.pattern.Match;

println(is_match("(ab)+c", "ababc"));            // true
println(is_match("\\d{3}-\\d{4}", "555-1234"));  // true
println(find_at("script", "firescript", 4));     // 6
println(last_error("[ab"));                      // unmatched '[' in pattern

m: Match = find_first("(\\w+)@(\\w+)", "mail me@host now", 0);
println(m.group(1));                             // me
println(m.group(2));                             // host
println(replace("(\\w+)@(\\w+)", "me@host", "$2:$1"));  // host:me

docs.title: fn is_match(pattern: string, text: string) -> bool [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text: Returns true when the pattern matches the input text. Without anchors, the pattern must match the entire input; ^ and $ control anchoring explicitly. Matching backtracks fully, so any way of matching the whole text is found. An invalid pattern never matches.

docs.title: fn find_match(pattern: string, text: string) -> bool [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text: Alias of is_match. Named match prior to 0.6.0; renamed because match is now a reserved keyword.

docs.title: fn find_at(pattern: string, text: string, start_pos: int32) -> int32 [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text: Position-aware matching: returns the length of the match starting exactly at start_pos, or -1 if there is no match at that position (or start_pos is out of range, or the pattern is invalid). With a leading ^ the match can only start at position 0; with a trailing $ it must end at the end of the text.

docs.title: fn last_error(pattern: string) -> string [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text: Validates a pattern and returns an empty string when the pattern is usable. If validation fails, it returns a short error message (see Errors).

docs.title: fn find_first(pattern: string, text: string, start_pos: int32) -> Match [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text: Finds the leftmost match starting at or after start_pos (a negative start_pos is treated as 0). The result is always a Match; check found() to see whether anything matched. An invalid pattern never matches.

docs.title: fn find_all(pattern: string, text: string) -> ArrayList<Match> [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text:
Returns every non-overlapping match, left to right. An empty match advances the scan by one character, so the scan always terminates (find_all("x*", "abc") yields four empty matches, at 0, 1, 2 and 3). An invalid pattern yields an empty list.

ArrayList<Match> holds an Owned element type, so read it with removeLast() rather than get() (see Collections). removeLast() returns the last match first:

all: ArrayList<Match> = find_all("\\d+", "a1b22c333");
while (all.size() > 0) {
    m: Match = all.removeLast();
    println(m.group(0));   // 333, then 22, then 1
}

docs.title: fn replace(pattern: string, text: string, replacement: string) -> string [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text:
Replaces every non-overlapping match with replacement and returns the result. In the replacement:

  • $0 .. $9 insert that capture group ($0 is the whole match). A group number past the last group, or a group that did not take part in the match, inserts nothing.
  • $$ is a literal $.
  • Any other $ is a literal $.

Empty matches are replaced too (replace("x*", "abc", "-") is -a-b-c-). An invalid pattern returns the text unchanged.

docs.title: Match [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text:
@firescript/std.regex.pattern.Match, returned by find_first and held in the list from find_all. Group 0 is the whole match; groups are numbered by their opening (, left to right.

  • fn found(&this) -> bool — false when nothing matched. On a no-match Match, start()/end()/group_start()/group_end() return -1, group_count() returns 0 and group(i) returns "".
  • fn start(&this) -> int32 / fn end(&this) -> int32 — offsets of the match in the searched text (end is exclusive).
  • fn group(&this, i: int32) -> string — the text matched by group i. Returns "" for a group that did not take part in the match (for example the unused side of an alternation, or a group quantified to zero repetitions), and for an out-of-range i. Use group_start(i) >= 0 to tell "did not participate" apart from "matched the empty string".
  • fn group_start(&this, i: int32) -> int32 / fn group_end(&this, i: int32) -> int32 — offsets of group i in the searched text, or -1 if the group did not take part or i is out of range.
  • fn group_count(&this) -> int32 — number of capture groups in the pattern, not counting group 0.

A group inside a repeated group ((ab)+, (a|b){2,3}) reports its last repetition.

docs.title: RegexPattern [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text:
The RegexPattern class (@firescript/std.regex.pattern.RegexPattern) compiles a pattern once and lets you search repeatedly:

import @firescript/std.regex.pattern.RegexPattern;
import @firescript/std.regex.pattern.Match;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

p: RegexPattern = RegexPattern("[a-z]+");
println(p.is_match("firescript"));
println(p.find_at("firescript", 4));
m: Match = p.find_first("123 abc", 0);
println(m.group(0));   // abc

Methods:

  • fn is_match(&this, &text: string) -> bool
  • fn matches(&this, &text: string) -> bool — alias of is_match
  • fn find_at(&this, &text: string, start_pos: int32) -> int32
  • fn find_first(&this, &text: string, start_pos: int32) -> Match
  • fn find_all(&this, &text: string) -> ArrayList<Match>
  • fn replace(&this, &text: string, &replacement: string) -> string
  • fn group_count(&this) -> int32 — number of capture groups (0 for an invalid pattern)
  • fn last_error(&this) -> string — pattern validation error, or empty string

The free functions each build a RegexPattern per call; construct one yourself to reuse it.

docs.title: Supported Syntax
docs.text:
All of the following is [IMPLEMENTED]:

  • Literals like abc
  • Escapes \n, \t, \r, and escaped metacharacters (\., \(, \\, \{, ...). An escape of any other character stands for that character.
  • Wildcard . (any single byte, including newline)
  • Anchors: a leading ^ (start of text) and a trailing $ (end of text). A trailing \$ is a literal dollar. A ^ or $ anywhere else is an ordinary literal character, and a pattern with nothing between its anchors (^, $, ^$) is reported as empty.
  • Capturing groups ( ... ) and non-capturing groups (?: ... ), which can be nested and quantified
  • Alternation with |; the leftmost alternative that leads to an overall match wins, and an alternative may be empty (a|)
  • Quantifiers *, +, ? (greedy)
  • Counted quantifiers {n}, {n,}, {n,m} on any atom or group (n and m up to 1000). {n,m} requires n <= m.
  • Character classes [abc], [^abc], ranges [a-z] (over any byte values), and shorthand classes inside a class ([\d_], [^\s]). A - just before the closing ] (or first in the class) is a literal.
  • Shorthand classes, inside or outside [...]:
Escape Matches \d / \D an ASCII digit / anything else \w / \W [A-Za-z0-9_] / anything else \s / \S space, \t, \n, \v, \f, \r / anything else

Matching works on bytes, so non-ASCII text is matched byte by byte.

docs.title: Matching semantics
docs.text:
Matching is a backtracking search: leftmost, with greedy quantifiers that give characters back when the rest of the pattern needs them. Alternation tries alternatives left to right. A repetition of something that can match the empty string ((a*)*) stops as soon as an iteration consumes nothing, so it always terminates.

Because it is a backtracking matcher, a pattern with nested unbounded quantifiers can take exponential time on adversarial input, and a repeat whose body is a group uses native stack per iteration: a single greedy repeat over several thousand characters can overflow the 1 MiB stack. A counted quantifier is expanded into copies of its atom, so (a{1000}){1000} is rejected as pattern too large.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Pattern errors are reported at runtime via last_error; there is no compile-time pattern validation yet. Searches with an invalid pattern never match. The messages are:

Message Cause pattern is empty empty pattern, or nothing between the anchors dangling escape at end of pattern a trailing \ unmatched '[' in pattern a class with no closing ] empty character class [] invalid range in character class a reversed range ([z-a]) or a shorthand as a range end ([a-\d]) unmatched '(' in pattern / unmatched ')' in pattern unbalanced parentheses unsupported group syntax (? followed by anything but : (lookarounds, named groups, flags) quantifier without target a *, +, ? or { with nothing to repeat (*a, (+), a|*) nested or non-greedy quantifiers are not supported a**, a+?, a{2}{3} unterminated '{' in pattern { with no closing } invalid counted quantifier malformed count (a{}, a{,3}, a{x}) counted quantifier minimum exceeds maximum a{3,1} counted quantifier too large a count above 1000 pattern too large the compiled pattern would exceed the size limit

docs.title: Not Supported Yet
docs.text:
• Lookahead and lookbehind ((?=...), (?!...), (?<=...)) [PLANNED]
  • Non-greedy quantifiers (*?, +?, ??, {n,m}?) [PLANNED]
  • Backreferences (\1) [PLANNED]
  • Named groups ((?<name>...)) and inline flags ((?i)) [PLANNED]
  • Word-boundary and other anchors inside a pattern (\b, \A, \z, ^/$ in the middle) [PLANNED]
  • Unicode-aware classes and case-insensitive matching [PLANNED]
  • Compile-time pattern validation [PLANNED]

docs.title: Future Sections [PLANNED]
docs.text:
• Linear-time matching (NFA/DFA simulation) for patterns that backtrack badly
  • Named capture groups and iteration over matches

docs.title: Text (std.text)
docs.text:
The std.text module provides StringBuilder (efficient accumulation of many string fragments) and split (dividing a string on a delimiter).

Status: StringBuilder (append/length/build) and split are both [IMPLEMENTED] and tested.

docs.title: StringBuilder
docs.text:
class StringBuilder {
    fn StringBuilder(initial: string);

    fn append(&mut this, s: string) -> void;
    fn length(&this) -> int32;
    fn build(&mut this) -> string;
}

Example:

import @firescript/std.text.StringBuilder;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

sb: StringBuilder = StringBuilder("");
sb.append("Hello");
sb.append(", ");
sb.append("World");
sb.append("!");
println(sb.length());  // 13
println(sb.build());   // Hello, World!
println(sb.length());  // 0 -- build() drains the builder

Methods:

  • append(s): Adds s to the end of the accumulated content. Takes ownership of s (matching ArrayList<T>.add()).
  • length(): Total character count of everything appended so far, tracked incrementally (not recomputed by summing fragments).
  • build(): Joins every appended fragment into a single string and returns it, draining the builder -- length() reads 0 immediately afterward. Not safe to call more than once expecting cumulative content; append more first if you need to keep building.

Note: StringBuilder has no zero-argument constructor -- pass "" to start empty (StringBuilder("")). This predates a fix to bare ClassName() constructor-call resolution (see tests/sources/classes/classes_zero_arg_constructor_bare_call.fire) and was kept as-is since there's no functional need to change it.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text: StringBuilder is backed by an ArrayList<string> of fragments rather than a raw growable byte buffer -- string primitives (std/internal/strings.fire) have no way to construct a ArrayList<T> themselves (internal runtime files carry no import statements), so building on the already-public ArrayList<T> was the straightforward option. build() drains fragments with ArrayList<T>.removeLast() rather than get()/enumerate(), which aren't safe for an Owned element type like string (see Collections's note on get()).

docs.title: split
docs.text:
fn split(&s: string, &delim: string) -> ArrayList<string>;

Splits s on every occurrence of delim, including leading, trailing, and adjacent empty fields. An empty delim returns a single-element ArrayList containing the whole string unchanged. If delim never occurs, the result is a single-element ArrayList containing s.

Example:

import @firescript/std.text.split;
import @firescript/std.collections.ArrayList;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

parts: ArrayList<string> = split("a,bb,ccc", ",");
println(parts.size());  // 3
println(parts.removeLast());     // ccc -- removeLast() drains in reverse order
println(parts.removeLast());     // bb
println(parts.removeLast());     // a

Note: split isn't a .split() dot-method on string like .indexOf()/ .substring()/etc. (see the strings feature table entry for the full list) -- it needs to return ArrayList<string>, and the compiler's @builtin_method dispatch (used for those other string methods) only supports backing functions defined in std/internal/, which can't reference ArrayList<T> (a normal importable module, not an internal runtime file). Called as a plain function instead: split(s, delim).

docs.title: Usage Notes
docs.text: • Draining an ArrayList<string> (via StringBuilder.build() internally, or directly from split's result) should always go through removeLast(), never get()/enumerate() -- see Collections for why.

docs.title: Generic Types (std.types)
docs.text:
The std.types module provides generic container and utility types.

Status: Pair, CopyablePair, Option, CopyableOption, Result, and CopyableResult are all [IMPLEMENTED] and tested.

docs.title: Pair<T, U>
docs.text:
A pair of values of potentially different types.

class Pair<T, U> {
    first: T;
    second: U;

    fn Pair(first: T, second: U);
}

Example:

import @firescript/std.types.Pair;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

pair: Pair<int32, string> = Pair<int32, string>(42, "answer");
println(pair.first);   // 42
println(pair.second);  // answer

Note: Pair is an Owned type; values are moved, not copied.

docs.title: CopyablePair<T, U>
docs.text:
A copyable variant of Pair for use with copyable types only.

copyable class CopyablePair<T, U> {
    first: T;
    second: U;

    fn CopyablePair(first: T, second: U);
}

Example:

import @firescript/std.types.CopyablePair;

coord: CopyablePair<float64, float64> = CopyablePair<float64, float64>(3.14, 2.71);
copy: CopyablePair<float64, float64> = coord;  // copies

docs.title: Option<T> [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text:
An optional value of type T. Use this to represent potentially missing values without explicit nullability.

class Option<T?> {
    value: T?;

    fn Option(value: T?);

    fn isSome() -> bool;
    fn isNone() -> bool;

    static fn Some(value: T) -> Option<T>;
    static fn None() -> Option<T>;

    fn unwrapOr(&mut this, default: T) -> T;
}

Methods:

  • isSome(): Returns true if a value is present
  • isNone(): Returns true if no value is present
  • Some(value): Static factory for a present value. Infers T from value, so it works bare (Option.Some(5)).
  • None(): Static factory for an absent value. Takes no argument to infer T from — use the explicit form, Option<int32>.None().
  • unwrapOr(default): Returns the value if present, else default. Drains the Option — extracts the value by nulling out the field, so isSome() reads false immediately afterward. Safe for any T, including Owned types (the same aliasing hazard ArrayList<T>.get() has for an Owned element is avoided here the way ArrayList<T>.removeLast() avoids it — see Collections).

Example:

import @firescript/std.types.Option;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

maybe_name: Option<string> = Option.Some("Alice");
if (maybe_name.isSome()) {
    println(maybe_name.unwrapOr("unknown"));
}

nothing: Option<string> = Option<string>.None();
println(nothing.unwrapOr("fallback"));  // fallback

Note: Option is an Owned type; construct carefully with move semantics in mind.

docs.title: CopyableOption<T> [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text:
A copyable variant of Option for copyable types.

copyable class CopyableOption<T?> {
    value: T?;

    fn CopyableOption(value: T?);

    fn isSome() -> bool;
    fn isNone() -> bool;

    static fn Some(value: T) -> CopyableOption<T>;
    static fn None() -> CopyableOption<T>;

    fn unwrapOr(default: T) -> T;
}

unwrapOr here doesn't drain anything — Copyable values are just read, not extracted, so the option is left intact and can be read again.

Example:

import @firescript/std.types.CopyableOption;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

maybe_count: CopyableOption<int32> = CopyableOption.Some(5);
println(maybe_count.unwrapOr(0));

docs.title: Result<T,E> [IMPLEMENTED]
docs.text:
A value that is either a success (T) or a failure (E). Use this to represent operations that can fail without relying on exceptions or sentinel values.

class Result<T?, E?> {
    value: T?;
    error: E?;

    fn Result(value: T?, error: E?);

    fn isOk() -> bool;
    fn isErr() -> bool;

    static fn Ok(value: T) -> Result<T, E>;
    static fn Err(error: E) -> Result<T, E>;

    fn unwrapOr(&mut this, default: T) -> T;
}

Methods:

  • isOk(): Returns true if the result holds a success value
  • isErr(): Returns true if the result holds an error value
  • Ok(value) / Err(error): Static factories. Neither infers both type parameters from its own argument (Ok never mentions E; Err never mentions T) — always use the explicit form, Result<T,E>.Ok(x) / Result<T,E>.Err(e).
  • unwrapOr(default): Returns the success value if present, else default. Drains the Result the same way Option<T>.unwrapOr() does — see its note above.
import @firescript/std.types.Result;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

fn tryDivide(a: int32, b: int32) -> Result<int32, string> {
    if (b == 0) {
        return Result<int32, string>.Err("division by zero");
    }
    return Result<int32, string>.Ok(a / b);
}

outcome: Result<int32, string> = tryDivide(10, 0);
println(outcome.unwrapOr(-1));  // -1

Note: Result is an Owned type; construct carefully with move semantics in mind.

docs.title: CopyableResult<T,E> [IMPLEMENTED]

A copyable variant of Result for copyable types.

copyable class CopyableResult<T?, E?> {
    value: T?;

    fn CopyableResult(value: T?, error: E?);

    fn isOk() -> bool;
    fn isErr() -> bool;

    static fn Ok(value: T) -> CopyableResult<T, E>;
    static fn Err(error: E) -> CopyableResult<T, E>;

    fn unwrapOr(default: T) -> T;

Example:

import @firescript/std.types.CopyableResult;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

parsed: CopyableResult<int32, bool> = CopyableResult<int32, bool>.Ok(42);
println(parsed.unwrapOr(-1));

docs.title: Usage Notes
docs.text:
• Prefer CopyablePair, CopyableOption, and CopyableResult for numeric/scalar types to avoid unnecessary moves.
  • Use owned variants for containers or strings that you want to pass around differently.
  • Both variants support generic type parameters; compile-time monomorphization produces efficient code.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import @firescript/std.types.Pair;
import @firescript/std.io.println;

// Pair usage
user: Pair<int32, string> = Pair<int32, string>(1, "alice");
println("User ID: " + (user.first as string));
println(user.second);
